question: You have just narrated Pennard to 2.5× at an 8× exit. The interviewer leans in: "how much is one turn of the exit multiple worth?" Answer it without restarting the walk.
model_answer_md:
One turn of the exit multiple is one extra (or missing) multiple on final-year EBITDA, and it lands entirely on the equity — the debt is owed regardless.

$$1\times \text{ on } £63.8\text{m of exit EBITDA} = \mathbf{±£63.8m \text{ of equity}}$$

On the £160m cheque that is

$$\frac{63.8}{160} \approx \mathbf{±0.4\times \text{ of money multiple}}$$

So: 9× takes the deal from 2.47× to about 2.9× (IRR toward 24 %); 7× drops it to about 2.07× (IRR toward 15–16 %). Roughly four or five points of IRR per turn, either direction.

The follow-through that earns the mark: this sensitivity is why the base case holds the multiple flat. A swing that size, controlled entirely by market conditions at the time of sale, is not something a committee will let the plan depend on — the walk has to clear its hurdle before the weather is consulted.
key_points: ±1× on exit EBITDA of £63.8m = ±£63.8m of equity, pound for pound
On a £160m cheque, ≈ ±0.4× of MoM per turn
Roughly ±4–5 IRR points per turn on this deal
The debt absorbs none of it — the swing is all equity
This sensitivity is the argument for underwriting a flat multiple

follow_ups.question: Why do sponsors underwrite a flat exit multiple when history says multiples often rise?
follow_ups.answer_md: Because the base case is a promise to the investment committee, not a forecast. The exit multiple is set by conditions five years out that nobody can influence — rates, sentiment, who else is bidding — so building it into the plan converts a controllable deal into a market bet levered five times. Assuming flat means the deal must work on growth and cash generation alone; any expansion that arrives is upside on top. It also disciplines entry pricing: a sponsor who needs 9× at exit to justify 8× at entry is really saying the price is too high today.

follow_ups.question: Which would you rather stress: the exit multiple or the growth rate?
follow_ups.answer_md: Stress both, but fear the multiple. A point of annual growth compounds to about £3m of exit EBITDA on Pennard — worth roughly £25m at 8×, well under half a turn's £63.8m. And the two are correlated in the wrong direction: the conditions that compress exit multiples are usually the ones that slow growth too, so the stresses arrive together. The growth lever at least responds to management action; the multiple responds to nothing the sponsor does.

weak_answer_note: Re-running the whole model instead of reasoning at the margin, or applying the turn to entry EBITDA (£50m) rather than exit EBITDA (£63.8m). The one-line answer — a turn is £63.8m, all of it equity, about 0.4× of MoM — is the fluency being tested.
